passage:
Subject: About Sunday

Dear Mridul,

I keep thinking about Sunday on the hostel roof. You told me the placement interview didn't go through, and I could feel the sentence "there will be other chances" sitting in my mouth, ready to go. I swallowed it. Instead I said, "You sound really disappointed." You went quiet, then said, "I practised for weeks." And after that everything came out, the questions you had blanked on, the part that stung most. I only nodded and stayed. Thank you for trusting me with it. Next time you want ideas, just say so, and I'll gladly help.

Vikas

qa.q: Where were Vikas and Mridul on Sunday?
qa.a: On the hostel roof.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when the sentence "there will be other chances" was sitting in the mouth?
qa.a: An urge to reassure and fix things quickly. Vikas felt that, and chose to swallow it and reflect Mridul's feeling instead.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that let Mridul go deeper?
qa.a: Vikas named the emotion by saying "You sound really disappointed," then stayed and nodded instead of offering quick comfort.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel after hearing "You sound really disappointed"?
qa.a: Understood, and safe enough to say more. Mridul answered "I practised for weeks" and then shared the questions that had been blanked on.

grounding: A young adult reflects Mridul's emotion back instead of reassuring, and Mridul goes deeper.

passage:
Host: So what did you do when Binita came back from her viva?

Yogesh: Honestly, my first thought was to say "Don't worry, you always do well." I'm Yogesh, by the way. But she was standing in the doorway with her bag still on, not saying anything, so I just said, "You sound really let down." She sort of laughed, and then she sat on my bed and said, "They asked about the one chapter I skipped revising." After that it went on for a long time. She talked about the examiner's face, and what she wished she'd said. I mostly said "mm" and "that must have felt awful." Later she said, "Thanks for not fixing it." That stuck with me.

qa.q: What did Binita say about the viva after sitting down?
qa.a: "They asked about the one chapter I skipped revising."

qa.q: What was Yogesh's first thought when Binita came back, and what did Yogesh do instead?
qa.a: Yogesh first thought of saying "Don't worry, you always do well," but instead named the feeling: "You sound really let down."

qa.q: What small step helped Binita talk more?
qa.a: Yogesh reflected the feeling in a few words and then mostly listened with sounds like "mm" and "that must have felt awful," rather than fixing anything.

qa.q: Why might Binita have said "Thanks for not fixing it"?
qa.a: Binita may have wanted to be understood first. Advice or quick reassurance could have felt like a way to move past the feeling.

grounding: A young adult tells the story of reflecting Binita's disappointment in words, and Binita talks more.

passage:
At the block office, Nikita noticed it about Manjula, a colleague, on Thursday. Manjula said "I'm fine" when asked about the file, but the shoulders were pulled up near the ears and the voice was flat, like a page read aloud. Lunch came, and Manjula ate alone at the desk, skipping the usual gossip about the tea stall. When someone mentioned transfers, Manjula looked at the stapler.
Nikita didn't say "Something's wrong, tell me." Instead Nikita carried two glasses of tea to the veranda and said, "You've been quieter since Monday. No pressure, but I'm here." After a pause Manjula said, "It's the transfer order. I didn't want to make noise." Nikita nodded and said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me."

qa.q: What did Manjula do at lunch?
qa.a: Ate alone at the desk, skipping the usual gossip about the tea stall.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when Manjula said "I'm fine" with tight shoulders and a flat voice?
qa.a: Nikita was concerned, sensing the words did not match how Manjula seemed, with shoulders pulled up near the ears and a flat voice.

qa.q: How did Nikita check in rather than assume?
qa.a: Nikita brought two glasses of tea to the veranda and said, "You've been quieter since Monday. No pressure, but I'm here," leaving room for Manjula to answer or not.

qa.q: What might Manjula be feeling about the transfer order and about saying so?
qa.a: Worried and reluctant to trouble anyone. Manjula said the order was not something to make noise about, and told it only after Nikita made it safe.

grounding: Nikita notices that Manjula says 'I'm fine' while body and voice say otherwise, and checks gently.

passage:
In the lab in Rotterdam, Hiroshi had shared a bench with a colleague, Ingrid, for a year, so the difference stood out. "I'm fine," said Ingrid, without looking up from the pipette rack. The voice was flat, the jokes had disappeared for a week, and Ingrid answered every question about the conference with "We'll see." Twice, a pause stretched out before the answer came.
Hiroshi could have guessed at the cause. Instead, at the coffee machine, Hiroshi said, "I might be wrong, but you seem tired lately. Is there anything I can help with, or would you rather not talk?"
Ingrid took a while. "Just a long week," Ingrid said. "But thank you for asking." Hiroshi nodded, and did not push.

qa.q: Where do Hiroshi and Ingrid work?
qa.a: In a lab in Rotterdam, sharing a bench.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi feel on noticing Ingrid's flat voice and missing jokes?
qa.a: Hiroshi was concerned that something might be wrong despite "I'm fine": the jokes had been gone for a week, and pauses came before replies.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi say "I might be wrong" before asking?
qa.a: To check rather than assume. The cues are only hints, so Hiroshi asked gently and allowed Ingrid to say no.

qa.q: What might Ingrid feel when saying "Just a long week" and then "thank you for asking"?
qa.a: Possibly touched that someone noticed, yet not ready to say more. It is unclear whether the week is the whole story, and Hiroshi accepts that.

grounding: Hiroshi sees a flat voice and avoidance behind Ingrid's 'I am fine', and checks gently instead of assuming.

passage: Avni skipped up to the swings in the colony park, where a girl with a red bag was sitting alone. "Hello!" said Avni. "I had poha for breakfast today. It had peanuts." The girl smiled. "I had bread and jam," she said. "What's your name?" asked Avni. "Lokesh," said the child. "Do you want to swing next to me?" Avni climbed on the swing beside Lokesh, and both pumped their legs higher and higher, saying "Whee!"

qa.q: What did Avni have for breakfast?
qa.a: Poha with peanuts.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when skipping up to the swings and saying hello?
qa.a: Friendly and eager. The skipping, the cheerful hello and the breakfast news show Avni wanted to connect.

qa.q: What did Avni do that helped start a friendship with Lokesh?
qa.a: Avni said hello, shared what Avni had eaten and asked for Lokesh's name, and then swung together.

passage:
"So, which class now, Maria?" asked Papa's cousin Zainab, passing the plate of pakoras.
"Fifth."
"And how are the marks?"
"Fine."
"Do you like your teacher?"
"Yes."
Maria stared at the plate. The questions felt like a queue at a counter.
Zainab tried again. "I saw a kite on the roof when I came in. Yours?"
"Yes!" Maria looked up. "It's a fighter kite, red and yellow. Papa built the frame." A giggle. "The tail was mine. It has ten knots."
"Show me after lunch?"
"Yes, come!"

qa.q: What class is Maria in?
qa.a: Fifth.

qa.q: What did the questions about class and marks feel like to Maria?
qa.a: Like a queue at a counter. Maria gave one-word answers and stared at the plate, which suggests boredom and a bit of pressure.

qa.q: What could Zainab try next time to help a child relax?
qa.a: Ask about something the child enjoys, as Zainab did with the kite question, rather than another question about class or marks.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when Maria suddenly lights up about the kite?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved that the conversation finally opened. Zainab changed the question, and Maria answered with energy and invited Zainab to see it.

grounding: A child at a relatives' gathering gives one-word answers to questions about class and marks, then relaxes when asked about a hobby.

passage: My name is Charu. At Nani's birthday lunch, my Masi Jaya sat next to me and said, "Which class? Marks good?" I said, "Sixth. Yes." She asked what the teacher's name was. I said, "Mrs Iyer." I kept looking at my glass and hoping the questions would end. It felt like a test I hadn't studied for. Then Masi said, "Nani told me you draw comics. Is that true?" I sat up. "Yes! A superhero who is afraid of the dark." Masi laughed and asked what the hero's name is. I talked all through dessert. I remember it as the moment I stopped counting the minutes.

qa.q: Whose birthday lunch was Charu at?
qa.a: Nani's.

qa.q: How did Charu feel about the questions on class and marks?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and eager for them to end. Charu kept looking at the glass and said it felt like a test not studied for.

qa.q: What turned the conversation around for Charu?
qa.a: Masi Jaya asked about Charu's comics, something Nani had mentioned, so Charu could talk about something Charu cared about.

qa.q: How might Masi Jaya feel after hearing about the superhero afraid of the dark?
qa.a: Interested and glad she found a topic that works. Masi laughed and asked more, which kept Charu talking all through dessert.

grounding: A child at a relatives' lunch gets class and marks questions, answers briefly, and relaxes when asked about a hobby.

passage:
Note from Mrs Nair, class teacher, after the Saturday picnic.
Bidisha sat on the edge of the group while Hrithik said, "Nice weather today, no?" Bidisha's mouth opened and closed. Later Bidisha told me, "It's such a pointless thing to say. Everyone knows it's nice weather." I said small talk isn't about the weather, it is a way of saying "I'm friendly, are you?" A low-risk test before deeper talk. Bidisha frowned, but listened. I suggested trying one simple line: "How was your weekend?" Bidisha said it aloud once to me. I will watch on Monday, and I will not push.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say at the picnic?
qa.a: "Nice weather today, no?"

qa.q: What was Bidisha thinking and feeling about small talk at the picnic?
qa.a: That it was pointless and fake, and probably a little scared, since the mouth opened and closed and no words came.

qa.q: What did Mrs Nair do to help Bidisha?
qa.a: Mrs Nair explained that small talk is a friendly low-risk test, suggested one simple line, and let Bidisha practise it aloud once without pushing.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the silence after the comment about the weather?
qa.a: Hrithik may just have been trying to be friendly and might wonder why Bidisha did not answer; Hrithik may not know it was nerves.

grounding: A shy teenager finds small talk pointless and freezes; an adult explains it is a low-stakes friendly test.

passage:
Thursday, after coaching class. I'm annoyed at myself. Ojas said, "Hot today, no?" while we were waiting for the gate to open, and I froze completely. In my head I thought, who says that? It's so fake. Why can't people just say something real? So I said "Yeah" and looked at my shoes. Silence. Then Ojas said, "I've been dying for a cold drink since morning," and somehow I said, "Same, I had a nimbu pani in my bag, and it's gone warm." Ojas laughed. And then we talked about the shop by the gate for ten minutes and the band whose poster is there. It wasn't deep, but it was easy. Maybe the fake part is what lets the real part in.
Sarika

qa.q: What did Ojas say while they waited for the gate?
qa.a: "Hot today, no?"

qa.q: What was Sarika thinking when Ojas talked about the heat?
qa.a: That it was fake and pointless, and worry that made Sarika freeze and look at the shoes.

qa.q: What small turning point let the talk start?
qa.a: Ojas kept going with a small comment about a cold drink, and Sarika answered with something real about the warm nimbu pani in the bag.

qa.q: What might Ojas be feeling when Sarika replies with "Yeah" and looks at shoes?
qa.a: Possibly awkward or unsure, though Ojas tried again with another simple line, which suggests Ojas was still friendly.

grounding: A shy teenager thinks small talk is fake and freezes, then finds it opens the way to an easy conversation.

passage: My name is Sarika. At last month's conference coffee break, I stood next to Vijay by the biscuit tray, both of us holding paper cups. My usual line, "So, how's the conference?", would have got the usual "Good, busy", and we'd have drifted apart. This time I said, "How did you end up in this field?" Vijay put the cup down. "I fixed my uncle's radio at ten, and never stopped," Vijay said, grinning. We talked until the bell for the next session. I hadn't planned anything clever. I was simply curious, and the curiosity did the work. On the stairs, Vijay said, "Let's continue at lunch."

qa.q: What did Sarika ask Vijay at the coffee break?
qa.a: "How did you end up in this field?"

qa.q: What was Sarika worried would happen with the usual line?
qa.a: That it would bring the usual "Good, busy" and lead nowhere, so the two would drift apart.

qa.q: What choice lifted the small talk into a real exchange?
qa.a: Sarika asked an open, curious follow-up question instead of a stock line about the conference.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel after answering the question?
qa.a: Pleased to be asked something personal and easy to answer, since Vijay grinned, talked until the bell and suggested lunch.

grounding: A person asks an open follow-up to lift small talk into a real exchange, with curiosity carrying the conversation.

passage:
Mentoring note, Thursday evening networking event, written by the programme coordinator.
Dhruv had told me beforehand, "I'm bad at this. I never know what to say." I stood back and watched. Dhruv joined a small circle where a caterer named Harsha was being asked about the menu. qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about before the event?
qa.a: Not knowing what to say, as Dhruv told the coordinator, "I'm bad at this."

qa.q: What could Dhruv do at the next event, based on what worked?
qa.a: Ask another open, curious question such as what got someone into their work, and follow up with one more, since no clever line was needed.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the question compared with "Lovely food"?
qa.a: It shows real interest in Harsha and not just politeness. Harsha's face changed and Harsha shared a story about a grandmother's kitchen.

passage: Bhavna, sit. I'm Tejas, and I will tell you about my first weeks at the mill office. It was lunchtime, twelve of us round one long table, and everyone was laughing about "Bapu's tea trick" and "the Tuesday lorry." I understood none of it. I ate quietly, smiling at the wrong moments, and told myself I'd sit elsewhere tomorrow. Then Mr Kulkarni, an old clerk, leaned over and said, "You don't know the lorry story, do you? Listen, it goes like this." He told it in one minute. After that, when the table laughed, I laughed too. He never made a speech about it. I'm telling you because on your first day, somebody did for me what you can do for the next newcomer.

passage:
Usha's first Monday, and the canteen was loud. Lunch break was only twenty minutes, and the team of six had squeezed round one table, all talking at once about "the Friday quiz" and "Rohan's hat." Usha held a tray of rice and kept nodding along, laughing a beat too late, not sure who Rohan was. With the clock ticking, nobody seemed to notice.
Noor did. Between bites, Noor said, "Sorry, Usha, inside joke. Every Friday we run a five-minute office quiz, and Rohan lost a bet about it. Do you like quizzes?"
"I do, actually," said Usha, sitting up. "I used to be on my college team."
"Then you're on ours this Friday," said Noor.

qa.q: How long was the lunch break?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling while nodding along and laughing a beat too late?
qa.a: Uncertain and a bit left out, since Usha did not know who Rohan was and was pretending to follow.

qa.q: What did Noor do in a short break that helped Usha?
qa.a: Noor explained the inside joke in a few words and then asked a question about whether Usha liked quizzes, inviting Usha in.

qa.q: What would probably change for Usha's first weeks if nobody had explained?
qa.a: Usha would likely keep smiling and feeling outside the group. Because Noor asked, Usha found something to share and joined the Friday team.

grounding: A newcomer listens to group lunch references they do not understand, and a quick explanation and a question include them.

passage: The rain had pushed everyone under the small shelter in the school garden, and the bell would ring soon. passage: On Salma's first day at the new school, the plan was clear in the head: sit next to the girl with the green hair band, then say "Hi, I'm Salma. Can I sit here?" All through the maths class, Salma rehearsed it, word by word. By break time, the sentence had become so big that it felt impossible. Salma ate lunch slowly at the end of a bench. Nobody came. Then Joseph, from the next row, sat down two seats away and said, "Are you new? I remember my first day." Salma's shoulders came down. "Yes," said Salma. "I kept meaning to say hi."

qa.q: What was Salma's plan for the first day?
qa.a: To sit next to the girl with the green hair band and say "Hi, I'm Salma. Can I sit here?"

qa.q: Why did the rehearsed sentence start to feel impossible to Salma?
qa.a: Salma kept rehearsing so long that the sentence felt bigger and scarier, showing a fear of being rejected.

qa.q: What could Salma try next time to avoid waiting so long?
qa.a: Say the simple hello early, before the rehearsal grows, since most people welcome a first hello.

qa.q: What might Joseph have wanted when sitting down two seats away and saying "Are you new?"
qa.a: To be kind and welcoming, remembering what a first day is like, and to start a conversation without pushing.

grounding: A child rehearses whom to approach at a new school and waits too long; someone else says hello first.

passage: I'm Vinita, and I sit two rows behind Kiran, who joined our class on Monday. This is what I saw. Kiran opened the lunchbox and closed it again. Kiran looked at our table three times and turned away three times. During the games period, Kiran stood near the wall with the ball in both hands, watching us, and mouthing something quietly, as if practising. I don't know what was going on inside. When I finally said, "Do you want to play with us?" Kiran said, "Yes!" so quickly that I was surprised. Now I say hello to anyone new before I overthink it, in case they are waiting too.

qa.q: What did Kiran do three times near the lunch table?

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling near the wall, holding the ball?

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when Kiran said "Yes!" so quickly?
qa.a: Surprised, as Vinita says, and probably glad, since Vinita now says hello to anyone new before overthinking it.

grounding: A child hesitates at a new school, and an observer sees that the first hello is welcomed.

passage: Coach's note, Tuesday. Tanvir stayed behind after nets and asked if he could talk. "Sir, I want to speak to Omkar," Tanvir said, "but he's the captain and everyone likes him. If I go first, won't I look desperate?" I asked what Tanvir wanted to say. "That the catch on Saturday was really good." I said that sounded honest, and simple honest lines often work better than clever ones. The worry, I think, is about being judged, not about Omkar. Tanvir practised it once, then took a breath and walked over. Omkar said, "Thanks, that ball was slippery!" and they talked kit bags until the bus.

qa.q: What did Tanvir want to say to Omkar?
qa.a: That the catch on Saturday was really good.

qa.q: What was Tanvir afraid of when asking to speak to the captain?
qa.a: Looking desperate by talking first to someone everyone likes, a fear of being judged.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped Tanvir decide to speak?
qa.a: The coach asked what Tanvir wanted to say and pointed out that the honest, simple line was a good one.

qa.q: How did Omkar respond to Tanvir?
qa.a: Omkar answered warmly, saying thanks and that the ball was slippery, and they chatted until the bus, so the first line was welcome.

grounding: A teenager fears talking first to a popular peer looks desperate, and a simple honest opener works.

passage:
Friday, 9 pm. I wrote three opening lines for Vikas on the back of my rough copy. One was a pun. One was about the physics test. One was so clever I crossed it out because it didn't even sound like me. All I could think was, what if he thinks I'm trying too hard? I kept picturing Vikas walking away. Then at the corridor stall today I just said, "Hey, I really liked your poster." Nothing else. Vikas smiled and said, "Thanks, I worked on it all week." That was it. I walked home surprised how ordinary it felt. Maybe simple was always enough.
Lalit

grounding: A teenager worries talking first to someone will look desperate, and finds a simple honest opener works.
